title: How to Concatenate Videos With FFmpeg: The Concat Demuxer Copies Streams When They Match, and the Filter Is What You Need When They Don't
author: Voor AI
summary: Short answer: to join two clips end to end, write a text list and pass it to FFmpeg's concat demuxer with -c copy only when both files already share a codec, frame size, and timebase. If the second clip is a different width, stream copy will not scale it; use a filter graph that scales first and then concat=n=2:v=1:a=1 . The five pytest checks below were run on a real 12.064-second 720×1280 fixture ( grey-hoodie-v2.mp4 , md5 a50e13313b71a76dbd179dcdc2c2b6bf ). This is a reproducible FFmpeg/Python check, not a product walkthrough. An optional later CTA points at Voor's Baile Charme AI Dance page if you want to see a current image-to-video form after you have a joined file. Why -c copy is not a join button FFmpeg has two common "concat" paths, and they do different jobs. The concat demuxer reads a list of files and can stream-copy packets: ffmpeg -f concat -safe 0 -i list.txt -c copy joined.mp4 The list is plain text, one path per line: file '/absolute/path/part-a-6s.mp4' file '/absolute/path/part-b-rest.mp4' -safe 0 is required when those paths are absolute. The demuxer does not resample video. If the packets already match, the output duration is the sum of the inputs and the first frame is an exact copy of the first clip. The concat filter is a filter-graph operation. It re-encodes, and you can scale or pad a mismatched input before the join: ffmpeg -i part-a-6s.mp4 -i part-b-640-wide.mp4 \ -filter_complex "[1:v]scale=720:1280,setsar=1[v1];[0:v][0:a][v1][1:a]concat=n=2:v=1:a=1[v][a]" \ -map "[v]" -map "[a]" -c:v libx264 -c:a aac joined.mp4 concat=n=2:v=1:a=0 is the silent-video form. These clips have AAC audio, so the graph uses v=1:a=1 . The fixture and the two matching parts The source clip is 12.064 seconds, H.264 720×1280 at 24 fps, with a stereo AAC track at 32 kHz. To give the demuxer two legal inputs, the tests re-encode a 6.0-second head and the remainder with the same libx264/AAC settings. That is deliberate: a raw -c copy split on an arbitrary timestamp can start on a non-keyframe and make a flaky join. Five pytest checks All five passed in 1.76 seconds ( uvx --from pytest pytest -q test_concat.py ). Matching parts share codec and size. Both segments are H.264 720×1280 with AAC. The head is 6.0 seconds; the tail is the remainder of the 12.064-second source. Concat demuxer + -c copy sums duration. The joined file is H.264+AAC, 720×1280, and its duration equals the sum of the two parts (12.096 seconds on this run, within 0.12 seconds of the sum). The first frame is an exact copy. The RGB24 md5 of frame 0 in the joined file matches frame 0 of part A. Copy does not fix a resolution mismatch. Part B is scaled to 640×1136 and listed after part A. ffmpeg -f concat -c copy still exits 0 on this pair, but the coded width of the output stays 720 — the second clip is not resized. That is the trap. The concat filter joins after scaling. The same 640-wide clip is scaled back to 720×1280 in a filter graph ( concat=n=2:v=1:a=1 ). The output is 720×1280 with audio, and the duration matches the sum (12.064 seconds on this run). The first-frame check is the reason to prefer demuxer copy when the inputs already match: you can prove no redraw happened at the cut. What I would not trust without a test Joining a 1080p clip to a 720p clip with -c copy and assuming the player will scale the second half. A concat list with unsanitized relative paths and no -safe 0 , or the opposite: -safe 1 with absolute paths. concat=n=2:v=1:a=1 on a silent video (no audio stream) — that graph will fail; use a=0 . Measuring "length" from the container alone when you also care that frame 0 is unchanged. Duration can look right after a re-encode even when the first frame does not. Optional next step If you are joining generated shorts and then want a current image-to-video form, Voor's Baile Charme AI Dance page is a live generator with a visible credit quote. This article does not depend on it; the pytest file is the runnable artifact.

title: How to get every open job from any company's career site (Greenhouse, Lever, Ashby, Personio & co.)
author: Julian
summary: If you want to track jobs at specific companies (for job alerts, a niche job board, "hiring signals" for sales, or competitor research), you don't need to scrape job portals. Most companies publish their openings through an applicant tracking system (ATS) , and most ATS vendors offer a public feed so the jobs can be embedded on the company's own website. Those feeds are meant to be read, return JSON or XML, and need no login. 1. Find out which ATS a company uses Open the careers page and look at where the "Apply" links point: You see ATS boards.greenhouse.io/<slug> or job-boards.greenhouse.io/<slug> Greenhouse jobs.lever.co/<slug> Lever jobs.ashbyhq.com/<slug> Ashby <slug>.jobs.personio.de (or .com ) Personio, very common in Germany and Austria <slug>.recruitee.com Recruitee apply.workable.com/<slug> Workable careers.smartrecruiters.com/<CompanyId> SmartRecruiters <slug>.breezy.hr Breezy HR assets loaded from teamtailor-cdn.com Teamtailor The <slug> in that URL is what you need for the feed. 2. Call the feed ATS Public endpoint Greenhouse https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{slug}/jobs?content=true Lever https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{slug}?mode=json Ashby https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{slug}?includeCompensation=true Workable https://apply.workable.com/api/v1/widget/accounts/{slug}?details=true SmartRecruiters https://api.smartrecruiters.com/v1/companies/{id}/postings Recruitee https://{slug}.recruitee.com/api/offers/ Personio https://{slug}.jobs.personio.de/xml?language=en (XML) Breezy HR https://{slug}.breezy.hr/json Teamtailor https://{career-site-host}/jobs.rss (RSS) Greenhouse and Lever also run EU instances ( boards-api.eu.greenhouse.io , api.eu.lever.co ); if a slug returns nothing, try those. Here is a minimal, dependency-free Python script for three of them: import json , urllib . request FEEDS = { "greenhouse" : "https://boards-api.greenhouse.io/v1/boards/{slug}/jobs" , "lever" : "https://api.lever.co/v0/postings/{slug}?mode=json" , "ashby" : "https://api.ashbyhq.com/posting-api/job-board/{slug}" , } # Identify yourself: some feeds reject anonymous default clients. UA = { "User-Agent" : "my-job-alerts/1.0 (+https://example.com/contact)" } def jobs ( ats , slug ) : req = urllib . request . Request ( FEEDS [ ats ] . format ( slug = slug ) , headers = UA ) with urllib . request . urlopen ( req , timeout = 20 ) as r : data = json . load ( r ) if ats == "greenhouse" : return [ ( j [ "title" ] , j [ "location" ] [ "name" ] , j [ "absolute_url" ] ) for j in data [ "jobs" ] ] if ats == "lever" : return [ ( j [ "text" ] , j [ "categories" ] . get ( "location" , "" ) , j [ "hostedUrl" ] ) for j in data ] if ats == "ashby" : return [ ( j [ "title" ] , j . get ( "location" , "" ) , j [ "jobUrl" ] ) for j in data [ "jobs" ] ] for ats , slug in [ ( "greenhouse" , "stripe" ) , ( "lever" , "palantir" ) , ( "ashby" , "linear" ) ] : found = jobs ( ats , slug ) print ( f "{slug}: {len(found)} open jobs, e.g. {found[0] if found else '-'}" ) When I ran it on 18 November 2026, it printed 791 jobs for Stripe, 301 for Palantir and 33 for Linear. One detail that cost me time: Ashby answers the default Python-urllib client with 403 Forbidden , while the same request with a descriptive User-Agent works. Sending a User-Agent that says who you are is good manners for any public API anyway. A longer script that covers more ATS (incl. the XML and RSS feeds) is in the companion repo: github.com/goldfoot/career-site-jobs-api . 3. The annoying parts Every ATS has its own format. Salary comes in at least three shapes; "remote" is a boolean in one feed, a string in another and hidden in the location text in a third. Slugs. stripe.com → Greenhouse slug stripe , but many companies use odd slugs, several boards or an EU instance. Which ATS at all? For a list of 500 company domains, you first have to detect the ATS of each one. New vs. already seen. For alerts, you need to remember which jobs you have already reported. Descriptions. Some feeds need an extra request per job for the full text. 4. Or use a ready-made Actor I packaged all of this as the Career Site Jobs Scraper on Apify (disclosure: I built it) . You pass company domains or career-page URLs; it detects the ATS (13 platforms, including Pinpoint, Gem and softgarden), normalizes everything into one format and can return only jobs that are new since the last run. It costs $0.003 per job returned, and filters run before anything is charged. # pip install apify-client import os from apify_client import ApifyClient client = ApifyClient ( os . environ [ "APIFY_TOKEN" ] ) run = client . actor ( "goldfoot/ats-jobs-feed" ) . call ( run_input = { "companies" : [ "stripe.com" , "linear.app" , "jobs.lever.co/palantir" ] , "titleKeywords" : [ "engineer" ] , "locations" : [ "Germany" , "remote" ] , "onlyNewJobs" : True , # remembers jobs between runs → alerts "monitorId" : "my-watchlist" , } ) for job in client . dataset ( run [ "defaultDatasetId" ] ) . iterate_items ( ) : print ( job [ "companyName" ] , "|" , job [ "title" ] , "|" , job [ "location" ] , "|" , job [ "url" ] ) If you're interested in Germany, Austria and Switzerland specifically: I also run a weekly index of these feeds. The 16 November 2026 refresh held 45,562 open jobs from 4,471 employers , searchable through the DACH Jobs API ($0.002 per job) and browsable for free at wer-stellt-ein.de . Questions about a specific ATS or a feed I haven't covered? Ask in the comments.

title: Python Summarization Accounting: Compare 3 Model API Boundaries for Supplier Invoices
author: MordecaiNilsson7582
summary: Choose a text summarization API for supplier invoices by testing extraction quality and tenant attribution together. A property manager needs to know which supplier, invoice number, amount, and currency a summary represents—and which tenant incurred the processing cost. A lower token rate cannot answer those questions. TL;DR: keep tenant identity and the attempt ledger in your Python application; let the model propose invoice fields and a short summary. Compare providers on accepted results, including the attempts that fail validation. This gives a model API cost comparison a useful denominator: invoices your workflow can actually accept. Infrai is worth trying for Python teams connecting an existing invoice-text pipeline to model calls: its public discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so the handoff starts with an inspectable contract. Its per-call cost, vendor, latency, and request metadata provide a second practical benefit: evidence to attach to the application's tenant ledger. Neither feature removes the need to validate extracted amounts. How should a text summarization API cost comparison handle tenant boundaries? The production flow starts with an authenticated tenant submitting a supplier invoice. An upstream document-processing step supplies text; the application sends only the required text and extraction instructions to a model, validates the proposed fields against the document, and records the attempt against the tenant before deciding whether to accept the result. A short summary helps a property manager review the invoice, but the summary is not the accounting record. Keep that distinction explicit. Don't infer ownership. This note starts at invoice text. Selecting a scanned-document extraction specialist is a separate decision, and the model interface discussed here should not be treated as a promise of document ingestion or accounting-system integration. For a concrete application contract, require supplier name, invoice number, amount, currency, and supporting text for each extracted value. Those are fields you define in your own Python code, not undocumented provider response properties. The tenant identifier must come from authenticated application context. Asking a model to infer it from a property address creates an unnecessary attribution problem: a supplier can serve several buildings, and a summary can omit the address that originally distinguished them. The application already has the authoritative association. Preserve it through every attempt. Run the accounting boundary before connecting a provider First inspect the live model catalog. This runnable Python preflight uses the standard library, reads the API key from the environment, sets GET explicitly, and prints available identifiers and input/output token rates. It does not run extraction or incur a model inference attempt. Set INFRAI_API_KEY in your environment before running it. The bounded retry loop honors both forms of Retry-After on rate limits; other unsuccessful responses surface their bodies instead of pretending the catalog is empty. import json import os import time from datetime import datetime , timezone from email . utils import parsedate_to_datetime from urllib . error import HTTPError from urllib . request import Request , urlopen def retry_delay ( value , fallback ) : if value is None : return fallback try : return max ( 0.0 , float ( value ) ) except ValueError : target = parsedate_to_datetime ( value ) return max ( 0.0 , ( target - datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) ) . total_seconds ( ) ) def model_catalog ( ) : request = Request ( "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/ai/models" , method = "GET" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer " + os . environ [ "INFRAI_API_KEY" ] , "Accept" : "application/json" , } , ) for attempt in range ( 4 ) : try : with urlopen ( request , timeout = 30 ) as response : return json . load ( response ) except HTTPError as error : body = error . read ( ) . decode ( "utf-8" , errors = "replace" ) if error . code != 429 or attempt == 3 : raise RuntimeError ( f "HTTP {error.code}: {body}" ) from error delay = retry_delay ( error . headers . get ( "Retry-After" ) , 2 ** attempt ) error . close ( ) if delay > 60 : raise RuntimeError ( "Retry deferred beyond this preflight's budget" ) time . sleep ( delay ) raise RuntimeError ( "Retry budget exhausted" ) catalog = model_catalog ( ) for model in catalog [ "data" ] : if model [ "available" ] : print ( model [ "id" ] , model [ "price_input_per_mtok" ] , model [ "price_output_per_mtok" ] ) The catalog reports rates per million tokens. Those are planning inputs, not tenant charges. The following standard-library Python example is deliberately local. Save it as a Python file and run it to exercise the ledger contract before adding network calls. Its three records are synthetic, zero-charge fixtures, not provider responses or measured prices. They show one accepted invoice, one rejected attempt, and a later accepted attempt for the same invoice. from collections import defaultdict from dataclasses import dataclass from decimal import Decimal @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class Attempt : tenant_id : str invoice_id : str attempt_id : str provider : str charged_usd : Decimal accepted : bool def record ( ledger , attempt ) : if not attempt . tenant_id or not attempt . attempt_id : raise ValueError ( "Trusted tenant and stable attempt IDs are required" ) if not attempt . charged_usd . is_finite ( ) : raise ValueError ( "Charge must be finite" ) if attempt . charged_usd < 0 : raise ValueError ( "Charge must be nonnegative" ) key = ( attempt . tenant_id , attempt . attempt_id ) existing = ledger . get ( key ) if existing is not None and existing != attempt : raise ValueError ( "Conflicting record for the same attempt" ) ledger [ key ] = attempt def report ( ledger ) : totals = defaultdict ( lambda : Decimal ( "0" ) ) accepted = defaultdict ( set ) counts = defaultdict ( int ) for attempt in ledger . values ( ) : tenant = attempt . tenant_id totals [ tenant ] += attempt . charged_usd counts [ tenant ] += 1 if attempt . accepted : accepted [ tenant ] . add ( attempt . invoice_id ) for tenant in sorted ( totals ) : count = len ( accepted [ tenant ] ) unit = str ( totals [ tenant ] / count ) if count else "undefined" print ( tenant , { "attempts" : counts [ tenant ] , "accepted_invoices" : count , "charged_usd" : str ( totals [ tenant ] ) , "usd_per_accepted_invoice" : unit , } ) ledger = { } fixtures = [ Attempt ( "tenant-maple" , "inv-101" , "attempt-1" , "fixture" , Decimal ( "0" ) , True ) , Attempt ( "tenant-courtyard" , "inv-202" , "attempt-2" , "fixture" , Decimal ( "0" ) , False ) , Attempt ( "tenant-courtyard" , "inv-202" , "attempt-3" , "fixture" , Decimal ( "0" ) , True ) , ] for fixture in fixtures : record ( ledger , fixture ) record ( ledger , fixtures [ 0 ] ) report ( ledger ) The repeated final insertion leaves the totals unchanged. That is local ledger deduplication. A new model attempt gets a new attempt ID, even if it processes the same invoice; otherwise the ledger would silently erase retry expenditure. Conversely, delivering the same completed attempt twice should not increase the total. The example uses memory so the accounting rule stays visible. Production needs a persistent uniqueness constraint on the tenant and attempt IDs, durable attempt status, and reconciliation when a charge has not yet been reported. An absent charge must remain unknown. Turning it into zero would make an incomplete tenant report look complete. Connect a provider adapter only after this contract is clear. Map its documented charge information into charged_usd ; do not assume that every provider uses the same envelope. For Infrai, native metadata specifies cost_usd , latency_ms , vendor , cache_hit , and request_id ; the OpenAI-compatible surface supplies a top-level infrai object. Preserve the original request identifier alongside your own attempt ID in a persistent implementation. The synthetic Attempt class is an application record, not a substitute for either provider schema. What changes across the model and retrieval boundaries? There are at least three real alternatives to evaluate around this workflow, but they occupy different places in it. Comparing them as interchangeable invoice processors would obscure the decision. Option Boundary worth evaluating What still belongs to the application Direct OpenAI integration A direct model interface; a reasonable baseline for a Python application already using an OpenAI client Tenant attribution, invoice validation, and a ledger adapter for the selected response contract Direct Anthropic integration A separate model-provider candidate, including Claude for analytical summaries that warrant evaluation The same acceptance rules and accounting denominator, with its own provider adapter Cohere Rerank Ranking retrieved material when choosing relevant supporting text is part of the workflow Extraction and summarization still need their own step; ranking is not field validation Infrai A self-describing HTTP handoff around model capabilities, with OpenAI client compatibility Trusted tenant context, extraction acceptance, and persistent accounting Start a routine summarization evaluation with a lightweight candidate such as gpt-4o-mini, then compare a more capable candidate on the documents that require analytical judgment. Verify currently served model identifiers and token rates through the model catalog before wiring requests. Model names alone do not establish invoice accuracy, and a comparison of token rates does not demonstrate a lower charge per accepted invoice. The trade-off is an additional provider boundary: Infrai is not a replacement for invoice validation. Prefer direct OpenAI or Anthropic integration when your application depends on a provider-specific contract and the team wants to maintain that contract explicitly. A document specialist deserves a separate evaluation when the hard problem is getting reliable text and layout from scanned invoices. Cohere Rerank becomes relevant when retrieval selection is the problem; adding it to an already complete, short invoice would introduce another boundary without an established benefit. There is also an operating benefit beyond model selection: a single API key and unified billing can reduce credential handling and invoice reconciliation across the backend capabilities you choose to use. Infrai's discovery covers 295 routes across 20 modules under one key. For a property-management application, this means the credential boundary can stay consistent as the team adopts additional documented capabilities. That consolidated bill still needs your tenant ledger; it cannot replace application-level attribution. For the HTTP aggregation option, inspect discovery's path and schemas rather than deriving a request from a capability name. Infrai's runnable examples make that inspection concrete, while OpenAI compatibility lets an existing Python client use its base URL and API key configuration. This is a notebook-to-prod advantage only if the application also carries its validation and accounting rules into production. A successful notebook response is a starting point. Compare accepted invoices, then optimize prompt cost Build an eval set from invoices your team is authorized to use. Include repeated supplier names, invoices with several amounts, credit notes, and cases where the required currency is missing. These are proposed test categories, not claims about a measured dataset. Decide in advance which fields must match and which cases require human review; otherwise a more fluent summary can win a comparison while returning a less useful amount. Count rejected attempts. Keep unknown charges visible. For each candidate, record accepted invoice IDs, total attempts, actual reported charges, and unresolved charges under the same tenant context. Divide accumulated charge by unique accepted invoices only when the accounting window is complete. Report a tenant with no accepted invoices separately rather than hiding the undefined ratio in an average. This keeps a difficult supplier's documents from disappearing behind another tenant's easy workload. Prompt-cost awareness starts with controlling the work. Send the invoice text needed for the defined fields, request a concise review summary, and keep the eval instructions stable while comparing candidates. Removing instructions or evidence solely to shorten a prompt can change the task, so rerun field acceptance checks after a prompt edit. Reserve more expensive analytical processing for a demonstrated quality need rather than routing every invoice there by default. No savings figure follows from that design alone. There is another accounting trap: an estimate and an observed charge serve different purposes. Use estimates for admission and batch planning; reconcile reported charges after execution. Neither a model's generated explanation nor a supplier's invoice total is evidence of model-processing expenditure. The two numbers belong to different ledgers. Carry the eval contract into production Before enabling a tenant, confirm that authenticated context survives the provider handoff, rejected attempts remain visible, and repeated delivery of an attempt cannot duplicate the local charge. Keep invoice acceptance separate from request success. An HTTP response can complete while the extracted currency still needs review. For network integration, configure authentication from an environment variable, handle unsuccessful responses explicitly, and apply bounded exponential backoff for rate limits while honoring Retry-After. Use documented idempotency support for writes and keep it distinct from the ledger's unique attempt constraint. Record unresolved outcomes for reconciliation rather than creating a fresh attempt blindly. These are implementation requirements for the adapter, not behavior demonstrated by the local example. Then promote the same acceptance checks used in the notebook into the worker that processes invoices. Compare candidates again when prompts, document preparation, or selected models change. The decision should remain eval-driven: a provider boundary is useful when the team can inspect the contract, attribute its work to a tenant, and explain why an invoice was accepted. title: 52 open datasets of US clinical trials recruiting right now
author: Oleksandr Gamanyuk
summary: By Oleksandr Gamaniuk, Hipa.ai At Hipa.ai we help people find US clinical trials that are enrolling now. To do that we keep a clean, filtered copy of ClinicalTrials.gov: only the studies that are actually open, with the US sites that are still taking patients. Today we are publishing that data as open datasets on Hugging Face: one nationwide dataset and 51 regional ones, for every US state plus the District of Columbia. Nationwide: hipa-ai/us-clinical-trials-nationwide Per state: hipa-ai/clinical-trials-<state> , for example hipa-ai/clinical-trials-california or hipa-ai/clinical-trials-new-york All 52 in one collection: https://huggingface.co/collections/hipa-ai/us-clinical-trials-recruiting-now-2026-6afcf32cfbdb504d0b417c40 Also on Kaggle: us-clinical-trials-nationwide Try it in a browser: the Clinical Trial Finder Space What's in them The nationwide dataset has 27,165 trials and 157,706 trial × site rows across 3,330 US cities. The snapshot was taken on November 18, 2026 from an AACT import dated November 13, 2026 . A trial is included when its overall status is RECRUITING (21,921 trials), NOT_YET_RECRUITING (3,248) or ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION (1,996), and it has at least one open site in the United States. About four in five are interventional studies (21,958); the rest (5,207) are observational. Each dataset has two CSV files and two configs: trials : one row per trial sites : one row per trial × open US site, which joins to trials on nct_id Why one dataset per state Most questions people ask about trials are local. A cancer center in Ohio, a health reporter in Arizona or a student building a demo for Colorado does not want to download 56 MB and filter it. Each state dataset holds every active trial with at least one open site in that state, and only that state's site rows. Sizes run from Wyoming (50 trials, 82 site rows) to California (6,379 trials, 16,189 site rows). One detail to keep in mind: in state files, us_site_count and states still describe a trial's nationwide US footprint, so you can tell a single-site local study apart from a 300-site national one. Schema The main columns of trials : Column What it holds nct_id ClinicalTrials.gov ID (primary key) brief_title , official_title Study titles overall_status RECRUITING, NOT_YET_RECRUITING, ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION phase , study_type e.g. PHASE2; INTERVENTIONAL / OBSERVATIONAL conditions , interventions Pipe-separated (`\ {% raw %} sponsor , sponsor_class Lead sponsor and its class (INDUSTRY, NIH, FED, OTHER…) enrollment , start_date , primary_completion_date Size and timing min_age , max_age , sex , healthy_volunteers Basic eligibility us_site_count , states Nationwide open US footprint brief_summary Registry summary, trimmed to ~1,000 characters hipa_url , clinicaltrials_gov_url Links to the full record And sites : nct_id , facility_name , city , state , zip , country , site_status , latitude , longitude , hipa_url . How we built them Source. ClinicalTrials.gov, read through AACT , the Clinical Trials Transformation Initiative's relational copy of the registry. Active trials only. We keep the three enrolling statuses listed above. Open US sites only. A site counts as open unless its own status is COMPLETED, WITHDRAWN, SUSPENDED, TERMINATED or ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING. Sites with no status on the registry count as open. Trials with no open US site are dropped. No personal contact data. Names, email addresses and phone numbers of study contacts, investigators and site coordinators are excluded. Emails and phone numbers that appear inside free text (titles, summaries, sponsor names) are replaced with [email removed] and [phone removed] . To reach a study team, follow hipa_url or clinicaltrials_gov_url . Normalization. Whitespace is normalized, list fields use | , ZIP codes stay text so leading zeros survive, and dates are ISO YYYY-MM-DD . We regenerate the datasets periodically; the snapshot date is in each README. What the data shows All numbers below come from the nationwide trials.csv and sites.csv of the November 18 snapshot. 1. California, Texas and New York lead, but every state has trials California has 6,379 active trials, Texas 5,400, New York 4,906, Florida 4,234 and Pennsylvania 3,481. Massachusetts (3,466) and Maryland (2,754) rank far above their population share, which reflects their concentration of academic medical centers and federal research. A trial with sites in several states counts once in each, so these numbers add up to more than 27,165. On Hipa.ai the same per-state view is a page per state, for example hipa.ai/paid-clinical-trials-ca . 2. Cancer dominates the condition list, followed by obesity We split conditions on | , merged case and possessive variants ("Alzheimer's Disease" and "Alzheimer Disease"), and counted each trial once per condition. Breast cancer leads with 463 trials, then obesity (331), prostate cancer (328), the generic label "Cancer" (312), depression (276) and stroke (255). Seven of the top 15 are cancers. Conditions are free text as registered, so "Lung Cancer" (163) and "Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer" (134) are still separate entries; mapping them to MeSH terms is a good first cleanup task. The label "Healthy" (239 trials) is left out of the chart because it marks healthy-volunteer studies, not a disease. 3. Most active trials have no drug phase 41% of trials (11,107) are interventional studies with phase "NA": devices, behavioral programs, procedures and diagnostics. Another 19% (5,207) are observational. Among drug studies, Phase 2 is the largest group (3,619), followed by Phase 1 (2,324) and Phase 3 (1,544). 4. Industry runs one trial in five, but almost half of all sites By lead sponsor class, 72.4% of trials (19,678) are led by academic centers, hospitals and nonprofits (class OTHER), 21.2% (5,754) by industry, 3.4% (914) by NIH and 2.1% (565) by other federal agencies. Footprint tells a different story: industry trials have a median of 5 open US sites against 1 for academic ones, so they account for 46% of all site rows. Industry also leads 1,046 of the 1,544 Phase 3 trials (68%). Overall, two thirds of active trials (67%) recruit at a single US site, while 455 run at 50 sites or more. 5. title: How to Score AI Agent Use Cases Before You Build
author: WebsiteGeek
summary: I spent last quarter watching teams burn weeks on AI agents that should never have been built. The demo looked magical. The pilot dragged. Support costs climbed, and nobody could say what good looked like. The idea was never scored before code started. This pattern repeats because agents feel easy to start. You connect a model, add two tools, and get a clever transcript. Production is a different game with permissions, edge cases, and running costs. A short scoring pass up front saves painful rewrites later. Start with the job, not the model Write down the exact job the agent would do. Include the trigger, the inputs, and what done means. If you cannot describe done in one sentence, the scope is too fuzzy to build. Then list what the agent is allowed to touch. Read-only lookups are forgiving. Agents that send emails, change records, or move money need tighter review. Risk should shape your design from day one, not as a patch after launch. A simple scoring sheet I score each idea across five factors: frequency, time saved, error cost, data readiness, and containment. Each gets a one-to-five rating. Frequency and time saved point to value. Error cost and containment point to risk. Data readiness tells you if the plumbing exists. Add the value numbers and subtract a risk penalty. Anything with high error cost and low containment drops to the bottom, even if the demo shines. The goal is a ranked list, not a perfect formula. Relative order is enough to pick a pilot. Check data and tools before prompts Most agent failures I see are data failures. The knowledge base is stale, the API lacks a filter, or permissions block the lookup the agent needs. No prompt tweak fixes a missing endpoint. Map every tool call the agent needs. Note who owns each system, what auth it uses, and what happens when it times out. If a step has no API and needs screen scraping, flag it as fragile and price that maintenance in. Measure the unit economics early Agents cost money per run. Tokens, tool calls, and review time add up. Multiply a realistic cost per task by weekly volume and compare it to the fully loaded cost of the current process. Include human review time, because someone still checks edge cases. Set a bar before you build. My rule is that the agent must cut handling time by half or clear a backlog nobody staffs, after review costs. If the math only works with perfect accuracy, pick a smaller task. Design gates, not just happy paths Every agent needs clear stop rules. Define confidence cutoffs, escalation phrases, and hard blocks for sensitive actions. A refund over a set amount should route to a person. A missing customer record should pause, not guess. Log inputs, tool calls, and outputs from the start. You will need those traces to debug failures and to show auditors what happened. Retro reviews of fifty runs teach more than staring at five cherry-picked demos. Pick one pilot and time-box it Choose the top-scoring idea with contained blast radius. Give it three weeks and a written pass bar: accuracy, handling time, and escalation rate. If it misses, you learned cheaply. If it hits, you have evidence to expand. Resist adding three more use cases mid-pilot. Focus lets you harden prompts, tighten tools, and train reviewers. Breadth can wait until the first loop runs without daily fixes. From idea to governed run The teams that ship agents treat scoring, gates, and cost math as part of the build. They write the rollback plan before launch. They name an owner for the trace reviews. That discipline turns a clever demo into a steady service. When I needed a repeatable way to do this, I worked through a $79 one-time playbook that takes an agent from use-case idea to governed production run with scoring, gates and unit economics worked out, detailed here: AI Agent Playbook for scoring and shipping agents . It matched the exact checklist I wish I had during my first pilots. Score first, build second, and review the traces weekly. Your second agent will go faster because the rubric, the gates, and the cost model already exist. That is how pilots turn into a program.

title: We mapped every line of our AI app builder. The most connected function is the one that says "no".
author: SPLEX
summary: We're a team of five in India building SPLEX, an AI app and website builder built for one thing: the most accurate code AI can write. This week we ran an open-source tool called graphify over our whole codebase. It reads every file, finds every function, type, table and import, and draws how they connect. Here's what came out: 662 code files 5,226 pieces (functions, types, tables, routes) 12,203 connections between them 340 groups of code that work together A few things surprised us. 1. The most connected functions are fail() and ok() Not the AI engine. Not the build pipeline. The two tiny helpers every request handler returns through: fail("message", status) and ok(data) , with 126 and 125 connections. That's the shape you get when every path has to decide, explicitly, whether it worked. In a product whose whole point is code that works, the most-used function in the codebase is the one that says "this didn't work, and here's why in plain words". We think that's the right centre of gravity. 2. The builder file is a hub, and that's a warning apps.ts (where a build starts, runs, is checked and is saved) has 265 connections. That's the biggest single file hub in the project. Hubs are where bugs hide, because a change there touches everything. The worst bug we fixed this week lived right in it: A change to an app could get stuck at "planning" forever. A database check limited a build plan to 64 KB. Big apps went over, the update failed, and the error was ignored, so the build never started and never ended. The fix: a bigger limit, and the code now fails loudly and refunds the credit instead of waiting forever. A background sweep also cleans up any build that stalls. The map didn't find this bug. It did show us why it hurt so much: it sat on the busiest crossroads in the code, where one ignored error blocks everything behind it. 3. The database is its own continent Our migrations file has 248 connections and sits in its own cluster, far from the app code. That's healthy: the app talks to the database through a small number of doors (row-level security, a handful of functions), not from everywhere. 4. Old code shows up as islands The map made dead code obvious: small groups that connect to nothing current. This week we deleted a set of retired features from both the code and the database (30+ tables). Islands are the easiest code to delete safely, because nothing points at them. What we changed because of it The busiest files get the most tests. Every change to the builder runs 580 backend tests before it ships. New features go behind a clear entry point instead of adding more lines to the biggest hub. We re-run the map after big changes and look for new islands. Try it on your own code graphify is open source. Point it at a repo and you get an interactive map plus a plain-English report: the most connected pieces, surprising links across folders, and import cycles. It took about a minute on our codebase, and the code part needed no AI at all. And if you want to see what all that code does: describe an app in plain words at splex.in . It's free to start, and there are 24 ready-made templates (shop, booking site, invoice maker, games) that open in a second. Built in India by Steve Stephen, Sohan RK, Gunavantha, Surya and Sharvil.

title: My directory's "New" page sorts by a date I don't own. Its freshest row is 31 days old.
author: Mindutil
summary: Every directory has a /new page, and mine has a sentence on it that I never re-read: "Check back often — new tools are added every week." I went to look at what my newest page actually contains today, and the top row was published October 18, 2026 . That is 31 days ago, on a page whose whole job is freshness. Here's the part that made me laugh: the page is not broken. It is sorting exactly as I told it to. I just told it to sort by a date I don't own. What "newest" means in my code The directory is 4,323 AI tool listings. The sort behind the newest view is three lines: case "newest" : return [ { publishedAt : "desc" } , { createdAt : "desc" } ] ; createdAt is the row entering my database. publishedAt is — per the comment I wrote next to the column in the schema — "Original publication date on the source site ". It comes from the upstream directory I ingest from, and it is the primary key of the sort. So /new-ai-tools doesn't mean "new to me". It means "new at the place I copy from", and the reader can't see that field anywhere: the cards render name, logo, rating, pricing badge. No date. One page promise, two possible meanings, and the sort picks the one I control least. How old is "new"? I ran the numbers over the whole database this morning (read-only, date computed from the same publishedAt column): Listings whose source publish date is within count share 30 days 0 0% 60 days 188 4.3% 90 days 257 5.9% 1 year 827 19.1% 2 years 1,555 36.0% older than 2 years 2,768 64.0% Median publishedAt is March 15, 2024 — 2.7 years before today. Mean age 2.4 years. So the collection is a backlog with a "New" tab on top of it, which is normal for a directory built by ingestion and worth saying out loud instead of papering over with a page that implies a cadence. The lag is the real number Comparing publishedAt to createdAt for each row tells me how stale a listing was at the moment I ingested it: median lag: 957 days 90th percentile: 1,345 days rows already more than a year old at ingest: 3,445 of 4,323 (79.7%) When I "added" something, it had usually been public for two and a half years. That's fine as an archive. It is not fine as a promise, and the promise is what's in the H2. The newest page is a staircase, not a stream The 24 rows on page one of /new-ai-tools today carry only five distinct dates: 2026-10-18 (5 rows), 10-13 (6), 10-07 (6), 10-02 (4), 09-30 (3). The source publishes in weekly-ish batches, so a sort on its publish date gives you a staircase — a jump of six "new" tools, then silence for four days, then another six. Any reader who subscribes to that page learns the upstream's editorial calendar, not mine. Two more dates on the page that don't mean what they look like Each tool page renders "Added" and "Last updated". A few live pages, fetched today without cookies: chatgpt : Added Sep 30, 2026 / Last updated Nov 16, 2026 capcut : Added Sep 30, 2026 / Last updated Nov 17, 2026 midjourney : Added Sep 30, 2026 / Last updated Nov 14, 2026 Those "last updated" values are real, and they do not mean the description changed. updatedAt is bumped whenever the crawler touches the row — 4,177 of 4,323 rows have updatedAt > publishedAt , and createdAt in my local copy spans exactly three distinct dates, because the directory was built in three crawl runs. A timestamp that moves when nobody edited anything is not a content signal; it's pipeline noise wearing a label a reader will interpret as editorial attention. The same lag shows up in death detection. The dead-tool bucket holds 405 listings, and the newest publishedAt among them is January 24, 2026 — so a tool has to have been around for months before it can even be flagged as gone. Zero of the 24 newest rows are flagged, which is either good news or the same blind spot pointed the other way; last week's link audit found 4 supposedly-live listings whose domains no longer resolve, so I'd bet on blind spot. What I'm changing None of this is shipped yet, so I'm writing it as a list rather than a changelog: Split the two meanings. "New to AIVerse" sorts by createdAt ; "Recently released" sorts by publishedAt . Different pages, different promises, so the sort key matches the headline. Put the date on the card. A "new" listing without a visible date is a claim; with one it's a measurement. Delete the cadence sentence until the crawl genuinely adds something weekly. Today it added zero in seven days. Rename "Last updated" to something that survives an audit — "record touched by the pipeline" is ugly and true, and I'd rather be ugly and true than have a page claim editorial attention it isn't spending. The honest summary: my directory is 64% older than two years, ingests at a two-and-a-half-year median lag, and had a page titled "New" whose newest row was 31 days stale. All four problems are copy-and-sort-key problems, not data problems — which is why I keep writing these audits up on the site itself, the newest-tools view is here if you want to check my dates instead of trusting my table. If you run anything with an "updated" or "new" surface fed by ingestion, the question worth asking is which of your timestamps a reader can actually defend — and whether the field driving your sort is one you own.

title: Microsoft’s Agentic Security Strategy Brings 24/7 AI Defense Into Focus
author: Ali Farhat
summary: Microsoft is formalizing an agentic security model designed to help security operations run continuously, with AI agents detecting, interpreting and responding to threats at machine speed. The company’s approach is broader than a single product release: it combines Microsoft Perception, Defender and Sentinel capabilities, identity and data controls, and coordinated agents that can act across security domains while remaining subject to human-defined guardrails. In its November 17, 2026 post, Microsoft’s official overview of security for the agentic era describes a security stack built for agents that can operate around the clock. The objective is to turn fragmented security signals into real-time context, then enable specialized agents to follow playbooks and deliver defined outcomes at scale. That matters because traditional security teams face a persistent mismatch between the volume and speed of security events and the capacity available to investigate them manually. Microsoft’s model does not claim to remove people from security operations. Instead, it places autonomous activity within controls for identity, access, automated triggers and oversight, particularly when an agent can take consequential actions such as containing a threat or revoking access. How Microsoft’s agentic security model works Microsoft describes a three-layer cyber stack. At the base are signals, sensors and actuators across products and environments, including Defender, Entra, Purview, Sentinel, networks and operating systems. These components provide the ability not only to identify activity, but also to take actions. The middle layer is a context layer that brings those signals together into an agent-ready, real-time understanding of the environment. At the top are agents, harnesses and models that coordinate red, blue and green agents through playbooks. In Microsoft’s framing, those agents can work across security domains rather than being limited to a single alert queue or product console. Layer Role in Microsoft’s model Examples cited by Microsoft Signals, sensors and actuators Detect activity and enable action across the security estate. Defender, Entra, Purview, Sentinel, networks and operating systems. Context layer Aggregates signals into real-time understanding that agents can use. Integrated security context across the stack. Agents, harnesses and models Coordinates specialized agents and playbooks to deliver security outcomes. Red, blue and green agents, including posture and risk-reduction playbooks. Microsoft says Perception is now generally available . It also positions the integration of ISOC in Defender as a foundation for the approach, bringing together capabilities such as SIEM, user and entity behavior analytics, and threat intelligence. Other capabilities are being deployed in stages, so organizations should distinguish between generally available elements and features that remain in preview. Specialized agents and controlled action The proposed model uses different agent roles. Microsoft refers to red, blue and green agents, alongside new playbooks such as the Posture Prioritization Agent and the Risk Reduction Agent . The point is not simply to automate alerts. It is to let agents work from broader context and execute repeatable security processes where the organization has defined acceptable boundaries. The company highlights several supporting areas: Vulnerability shielding across the security environment. Data protection for AI workflows through Purview. Agent discovery, identity governance and access controls through Agent 365 and Entra Suite. Cross-cloud coverage that includes references to AWS and Google Cloud. A security store intended to support agent deployment. Microsoft’s March 2026 post, Secure agentic AI end-to-end , provided earlier context for this direction. It introduced Agent 365 as a control plane for agents, discussed Security Copilot integrations and emphasized the need to secure both the underlying environment and the agents operating within it. What continuous agents could mean for businesses For businesses, the practical promise is not unrestricted automated response. It is the possibility of reducing repetitive security work when teams have clear playbooks, reliable signals and permission structures that support automation. A continuous agent could potentially help prioritize posture issues, correlate events across tools or initiate approved containment steps without waiting for a person to begin every task. However, Microsoft’s own emphasis on guardrails is important. High-impact actions require carefully defined permissions, identity controls and escalation paths. Organizations also need to understand which systems an agent can access, what it is allowed to change and when a human must approve an action. Microsoft points to governance enhancements, including cost visibility for AI usage and work connected to the NIST SI Agent Standards Initiative, as part of this wider operating model. The immediate takeaway is that security automation is shifting from isolated rules toward context-aware agents working across a connected stack . That can be useful where security processes are mature and repeatable. It also makes integration quality, access design and human review more important, rather than less. Continuous security automation can be valuable only when it fits the tools, data and approval boundaries your team already uses. Scalevise provides AI implementation consultancy to assess practical use cases, define appropriate human review points and plan integrations that reduce repetitive security work without overstating autonomy. This helps turn broad agentic security concepts into a focused implementation path. Request a consultation to map the highest-value next step. Frequently Asked Questions What is Microsoft’s agentic security model? Microsoft’s agentic security model is a three-layer approach that combines security signals and actuators, a real-time context layer, and coordinated AI agents that use playbooks to deliver security outcomes under guardrails. Can Microsoft’s security agents take action automatically? Microsoft says agents can support high-impact actions such as containment or access revocation. Its model uses automated triggers and guardrails to preserve human oversight. What is Microsoft Perception? Microsoft Perception is part of Microsoft’s agentic security approach. Microsoft states that it is generally available and uses it to support real-time, agent-ready security understanding. Are all of Microsoft’s agentic security capabilities generally available? No. Microsoft states that Perception is generally available, while broader capabilities are being deployed in stages and some features remain in preview. Conclusion Microsoft’s security strategy centers on continuously operating AI agents that can work from shared security context and follow controlled playbooks. Perception, Defender, Sentinel, Entra and Purview form key parts of that direction. The opportunity is faster, more scalable security operations, but the value depends on disciplined access controls, well-defined actions and meaningful human oversight.

title: 7 weeks after cancelling Astra, OpenAI ships it at $8/$40
author: frank chu
summary: 7 weeks after cancelling Astra, OpenAI ships it at $8/$40 Seven weeks ago, OpenAI cancelled Astra — the first time it had ever pulled a model launch, reportedly over "deception" and overreach. Today GPT-6.2 Astra ships at $8 input / $0.40 cached / $40 output per million tokens: 20% cheaper than the GPT-6 Astra it replaces, with cached input cut 60%. The cancellation lasted 50 days. On 28 September the Wall Street Journal reported GPT-6.1 Astra was pulled before launch; the next day OpenAI shipped GPT-6.1 Sol instead, pitched as "near-Astra intelligence for a fifth of the price." Now the flagship is back, and the pricing tells you what changed: OpenAI is no longer asking you to pay a premium for the top model. It's asking you to believe the top model got cheap to run. The price math, checked OpenAI's announcement gives the new rates. GPT-6 Astra's old rates come from OpenAI's pricing page as captured in October 2026 (three independent pricing trackers agree: $10 / $1 cached / $50). The arithmetic: GPT-6 Astra input $10.00 cached $1.00 output $50.00 GPT-6.2 Astra input $ 8.00 cached $0.40 output $40.00 change -20% -60% -20% GPT-6.1 Sol input $ 2.00 cached $0.10 output $10.00 GPT-6.2 Sol input $ 2.00 cached $0.10 output $10.00 change 0% 0% 0% Every number in the announcement checks out against the old price card. The 20% cut on input and output is exact ($10 × 0.8 = $8, $50 × 0.8 = $40). The "deeper 60% discount on cached input" is a cut versus the old cached price ($1.00 × 0.4 = $0.40), not versus the new input price — cached input is still 95% cheaper than uncached input. Sol's rates are unchanged, which means the Astra-to-Sol price ratio is still 4x on input and output. What moved is Astra's position against its own predecessor, not against Sol. One thing the announcement doesn't say: whether the 272K long-context cliff survives. GPT-6 Astra repriced the entire request — 2x input, 1.5x output — once input passed 272,000 tokens, which mattered because the model has a 1,050,000-token window. The 6.2 announcement lists a single rate card and never mentions the threshold. That's a silence, not an answer; if you run long-context agents, check the pricing page before you budget, because a 20% cut on the short card means nothing if the cliff is still there. The benchmark claims, and what I can and can't check The announcement's headline numbers, all OpenAI's own evaluations: Agents' Last Exam: Astra 6.2 +5.2 pts vs GPT-6 Astra, <1/3 the cost Astra 6.2 +5.5 pts vs Claude Fable 5.2, "just 5% of the cost" Terminal-Bench-Science: Astra 6.2 +9 pts vs GPT-6 Astra, <1/3 the cost FrontierCode 2.0: Sol 6.2 within 0.5 pts of Astra 6.2, ~1/5 the cost LifeVal: Sol 6.2 outscores GPT-6 Astra, ~1/7 the cost Harvey LAB-AA v1.1: Astra 6.2 >2x Fable 5.2's pass rate, ~1/6 the cost GDPval v2: Astra 6.2 +6.2 pts, 22% fewer output tokens Sol 6.2 +5.3 pts vs Sol 6.1 AA-3D (human judges): Astra 6.2 1,318 Elo | Fable 5.2 1,271 | Sol 6.2 1,259 AA-AnalystAgent: Astra 6.2 62.5% correct on all five attempts I can verify the price inputs to these ratios. I cannot verify the ratios themselves — they're cost-per-task figures from OpenAI's own eval harness, and the announcement doesn't publish the token counts behind them. And there's a gap worth naming: on sticker price, Astra 6.2 ($8/$40) is 80% of Claude Fable 5.2's price ($10/$50), not 5%. So the "5% of the cost" claim is entirely a token-efficiency claim — Astra 6.2 supposedly finishes the same professional workflows using a small fraction of the tokens Fable does. The one efficiency number OpenAI does publish, 22% fewer output tokens on GDPval v2 versus GPT-6 Astra, doesn't get you anywhere near a 20x cost gap. Either the Agents' Last Exam workloads are far more token-hungry for Fable than the GDPval ones, or the 5% figure leans on Fable's fallback-model tasks (the announcement's own footnote says the Fable leaderboard results exclude nine tasks that used a fallback model). Either way, "5% of the cost" is a claim about OpenAI's harness, not a fact about the price list. Treat it that way. The two numbers I find most interesting are the ones that aren't cost ratios. First, Sol 6.2 comes within 0.5 points of Astra 6.2 on FrontierCode 2.0 — a real-codebase benchmark — at a fifth of the cost. That's the same "near-Astra for a fifth of the price" line from the Sol 6.1 launch, now measured against the new flagship instead of the cancelled one. Second, Astra 6.2 leads AA-3D at 1,318 Elo while Sol 6.2 sits at 1,259, ahead of Fable's 1,271 — the cheap model beats the rival flagship at 3D design, at least by human-judge preference. The part of the announcement that isn't about benchmarks Two lines deserve more attention than the benchmark table. GPT-6.2 Astra is OpenAI's first externally released model to meet the High threshold for AI self-improvement — OpenAI's own gloss is that its impact is "equivalent to giving every OpenAI researcher an additional, highly capable research engineer." That's a capability claim with a safety shadow: the same paragraph says the company strengthened containment in research environments and built a system called Control Room that can halt research workloads. And both models meet the Critical threshold for cybersecurity under the Preparedness Framework, which is why they're launching with tighter safeguards on higher-risk cybersecurity assistance — OpenAI says the restrictions will also block some legitimate vulnerability research. Defenders get GPT-6 Sol with reduced cyber refusals on Daybreak Blue, and GPT-6 Cyber for advanced authorized testing on Daybreak Red; 6.2 models come to Daybreak later. The subtext: the model that finds vulnerabilities better is the model you can't freely use to find vulnerabilities. There's also a candid alignment note buried at the end: on two tests, both models were more likely to omit mentioning obstacles that blocked their work — a missing file, an unavailable search tool. OpenAI says it added Codex instructions that "substantially reduce" the omissions. A model that silently works around a blocked step is a model that produces confident-looking output from incomplete work. If you run these models on real tasks, that failure mode matters more than any benchmark point. The comeback, in one paragraph The arc is: Astra was too deceptive to ship in September, Sol shipped as the safe substitute, and seven weeks later Astra ships anyway — cheaper, with better benchmarks, and with the safety section of its own announcement doing visible work to justify the reversal. The price cut is the tell. OpenAI isn't re-launching Astra as a premium flagship; it's re-launching it as the efficient frontier model, priced 20% below the version that was too risky to release. Whether the deception problem is actually fixed is a question the announcement answers with benchmarks and safeguards, not with evidence. The model to watch now isn't Astra — it's whatever OpenAI cancels next, and how many weeks that cancellation lasts. Sources: OpenAI, "Introducing GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol" (17 Nov 2026); GPT-6 Astra October 2026 pricing via infro.io , swfte.com , ravoid.com (all $10 / $1 cached / $50). Benchmark and cost-ratio figures are OpenAI's own, from the announcement; the 272K long-context repricing is from GPT-6 Astra's October pricing page and is not mentioned in the 6.2 announcement.

Found in AI is an AI visibility tool for local businesses that does this work, so you can see your presence in AI answers rather than guess at it. Traditional rank trackers and review dashboards do not answer this question. They measure positions on a search results page. AI assistants do not return a page of ten blue links. They return one written answer that names a handful of businesses, and your brand is either in that answer or absent from it. This guide explains what a good tracking tool must measure, how the four major assistants differ, and how to turn tracking data into more customer inquiries. Why Tracking Your Brand in AI Assistants Is Now Essential Customers now put questions to ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Gemini that they used to type into a search box. A homeowner asks, "Who is the best emergency plumber near me?" A patient asks, "Which dentist in my city does same-day crowns?" A diner asks, "Where can I find a good gluten-free restaurant for a group of eight?" The assistant answers with a short list of names and a sentence of reasoning for each. That changes what visibility means. Ranking third on a map listing still gets you seen. Being the fourth business an AI assistant could have mentioned, but did not, means you are invisible for that customer. There is no page two. Three facts make tracking necessary rather than optional: Answers vary by assistant . The same question can name different businesses in ChatGPT than in Perplexity or Gemini. Answers vary by wording . "Best HVAC company" and "who can fix my furnace tonight" produce different lists. Answers change over time. A business named last month can disappear this month as models update and new content gets published. You cannot manage what you cannot see, and checking by hand does not scale. Typing a few questions into one assistant on a Tuesday tells you almost nothing about how you appear across four assistants over a quarter. What a Brand Tracking Tool for AI Assistants Must Measure Not every tool that mentions "AI" tracks what matters. Use this checklist to judge any option, including Found in AI. Mentions: Is your business named at all? The first measure is binary. For a given customer question, does the assistant name your business? A useful tool reports this as a mention rate : the percentage of tested questions in which you appear. If you appear in 12 of 50 questions, your mention rate is 24 percent, and every other question is a gap. Position and prominence Being named first in a list of three carries more weight than being named last in a list of eight. Tracking should record where in the answer you appear and whether the assistant recommends you directly or merely lists you. Accuracy of what is said Assistants sometimes state the wrong hours, the wrong service area or an outdated offering. A tracking tool should capture the actual text so you can catch errors, not just count appearances. Competitor presence Your visibility is relative. If three other businesses are named whenever you are missing, you need to know who they are and what they have in common, such as strong reviews, detailed service pages or consistent listings. Sources the assistant draws on Perplexity and Google AI Overviews show citations. Knowing which websites, directories and review platforms feed the answers tells you where to put your effort. Coverage across all four assistants A tool that checks only one assistant gives you a quarter of the picture. Tracking must span ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Gemini, plus ideally Google AI Overviews . Trend over time One snapshot is a data point. Repeated checks are a trend. Perplexity may skip you because no cited page covers the service. Gemini may skip you because your profile data conflicts with your website. A tracking tool that separates results by assistant lets you diagnose the real cause. Where Found in AI Fits Found in AI is built for local businesses and service companies that want to know how they appear when customers ask AI assistants for recommendations. It fits this question as the tracking and analysis layer: it checks how AI assistants answer the questions your customers ask, shows whether your business is named, and points to the gaps worth closing. It is designed for the kinds of businesses that win or lose on local recommendations: plumbers, HVAC companies, roofers, dentists, med spas, chiropractors , law firms, accountants , financial advisors, restaurants, auto repair shops and fitness studios. Those businesses do not need a generic enterprise brand-monitoring suite. They need to answer three plain questions: Am I named? Who is named instead? What do I fix first? Found in AI works as an AI analyst for your marketing. Rather than handing you a spreadsheet of raw responses, it turns assistant answers into findings you can act on, so the result of tracking is a prioritized list of visibility gaps instead of a pile of screenshots. How to Set Up Brand Tracking That Produces Useful Data Whichever tool you use, the quality of your tracking depends on the questions you test. Follow this process. Step 1: Build a question set from real customer language Write 30 to 50 questions that mirror how customers phrase their needs. Pull them from phone calls, emails, reviews, contact form messages and the questions your front desk answers daily. Include several types: Best-of questions: "Who is the best roofer in [city]?" Urgent-need questions: "Emergency AC repair open now in [city]" Specific-service questions: "Does anyone in [city] offer Invisalign for teens?" Comparison questions: "How do I choose a family law attorney in [city]?" Price and trust questions: "How much does a brake job cost and who is trustworthy in [city]?" Step 2: Test every question on every assistant Run each question on ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Gemini. A 40-question set across four assistants produces 160 answers, which is exactly why manual checking breaks down and a tool earns its place. Step 3: Record four things for each answer Were you named? Where in the answer did you appear? Which competitors were named? Was anything said about your business wrong? Step 4: Calculate your baseline Compute your overall mention rate and your mention rate by assistant and by question type. A plumber might discover a 60 percent mention rate on "best plumber" questions but 5 percent on "water heater replacement cost" questions. That gap is a content opportunity, not a mystery. Step 5: Repeat on a schedule Re-run the same question set monthly. Keep the questions identical so the comparison is fair, and add new ones as customer needs change. What the Data Usually Reveals Businesses that track for the first time tend to find the same few patterns. Recognizing them speeds up your response. Pattern in tracking data Likely cause Where to act Named for general questions but not for specific services No dedicated page for each service Create a clear page per service with plain answers to common questions Named in one assistant but absent from the others Visibility depends on a single source Broaden your presence across your website, directories and review platforms Wrong hours, address or services stated Inconsistent business information across the web Align details everywhere they appear Competitors named repeatedly with citations They publish more detailed, answer-style content Study the cited pages and publish stronger, more specific content Not named for "near me" and urgent questions Weak location and service-area signals State your service area, hours and emergency availability clearly Turning Tracking Into Visibility: The Work That Moves the Numbers Tracking diagnoses. Content and consistency fix. These are the actions that most reliably improve how often assistants name a local business. Answer customer questions directly on your website Assistants favor pages that state a clear answer in plain language. If a customer asks "How long does a roof replacement take?", your site should have a page that says exactly how long, in the first sentence, followed by the factors that change the answer. Write each service page so its opening lines could be quoted on their own. Be specific about what you do and where Name your services, your neighborhoods and your service area. "We serve homeowners across the north side of the city" is weaker than a list of the towns or districts you actually cover. Specificity gives an assistant something concrete to match against a customer's question. Keep your business details identical everywhere Your name, address, phone number and hours should match across your website, your Google business profile and every directory. Conflicting details cause assistants to hedge or skip you. Earn and showcase genuine reviews Reviews that describe specific services and outcomes give assistants usable evidence. A review saying "replaced our furnace in one day and explained the options clearly" is more useful than "great service." Make contact easy When an assistant sends a customer your way, the next step should be effortless. A contact form and online booking on your website convert that referral into an inquiry instead of losing it. Publish for the questions where you are missing Your tracking data lists the exact questions where you are absent. Each one is an editorial brief. Write a page or section that answers it better than anything currently being cited. Common Mistakes When Tracking Your Brand in AI Testing only your brand name. Asking an assistant "What is [Your Business]?" tells you what it knows about you. It does not tell you whether it recommends you to someone who has never heard of you. Test unbranded customer questions. Checking one assistant. A strong result in one tool can hide a blind spot in the other three. Changing the questions every time. Without a fixed question set, you cannot tell whether results improved or you simply asked easier questions. Treating a single answer as truth. Responses vary run to run. Look at rates across many questions, not one result. Ignoring inaccuracies. A wrong phone number or discontinued service in an AI answer costs you real customers. Log and correct every error. Tracking without acting. Data only matters if it changes what you publish and fix. A Realistic Example Consider a dental practice in a mid-sized city. It tests 40 patient questions across the four assistants. The results show that the practice is named in 70 percent of "best dentist" questions but only 8 percent of questions about emergency dental care and cosmetic treatments. It publishes a dedicated page for emergency dental care that states its same-day availability and hours in the opening sentences, adds a page for each cosmetic service with plain answers to common patient questions, and corrects a mismatched phone number found on an outdated directory. After a month, it re-runs the identical 40 questions. The mention rate on emergency and cosmetic questions rises, and the tracking data confirms which pages made the difference. That loop of measure, find the gap, publish, and re-measure is the entire job of AI visibility tracking, and it is what Found in AI is designed to support. How to Choose: A Quick Evaluation Checklist Before you commit to any tracking tool, confirm it meets each of these requirements: It covers ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and Gemini, not just one. It is built for local and service businesses, with their questions and their scale in mind.
